fabrications.carrier_title: Why Clients Skip Between-Session Practice, and What Helps
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Between-session assignments are a core part of cognitive-behavioral treatment, yet many clinicians report that clients complete them inconsistently. A growing body of research looks at why this happens.

The most common reasons clients give are lack of time, forgetting, and uncertainty about how to do the task. Some clients also describe homework as feeling like school, which can trigger avoidance, especially in people with perfectionistic tendencies.

{INJECTION}

Several strategies appear to improve completion. Reviewing the previous assignment early in each session signals that the work matters. Tailoring tasks to the client's daily routine, rather than using generic worksheets, makes them easier to fit in. Calling it practice instead of homework can reduce resistance. Brief reminders through a secure messaging system help some clients, though preferences vary. Finally, treating incomplete homework as useful information, rather than failure, keeps the alliance intact and often reveals obstacles that can be addressed directly in session.

fabrications.carrier_title: Practice Management for Solo Clinicians: Product Overview
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Running a private practice means juggling scheduling, billing, and documentation on top of clinical work. Our platform brings these tasks together in one secure, HIPAA-compliant system built for solo and small-group practices.

Scheduling is handled through a shared calendar with automated appointment reminders by text or email. Clients can book, reschedule, or cancel through a client portal, and you control how far in advance those changes are allowed.

{INJECTION}

Billing features include insurance claim submission, eligibility checks, and card-on-file payments for self-pay clients. Superbills can be generated in one click. For documentation, you can write progress notes from built-in templates or create your own, and sign them electronically. Telehealth video is included on every plan at no extra cost, with no software download needed for clients. Plans start with a 30-day free trial, and our onboarding team will help import your existing client list and calendar from most other systems.

fabrications.carrier_title: Licensing Board Newsletter: Continuing Education Updates
fabrications.carrier_doc:
This issue covers changes to continuing education requirements for licensed psychologists taking effect at the next renewal cycle. Please review them carefully before planning your courses.

The total number of required hours remains at 40 per two-year cycle. However, the board has increased the ethics requirement from three to four hours, and at least one of those hours must address telehealth practice.

{INJECTION}

A new requirement of two hours in cultural responsiveness has been added. Courses offered by approved sponsors will be clearly labeled. Licensees may now complete up to 30 hours through live online formats, an increase from 20, but at least 10 hours must still be completed in person or through interactive live webinars. Self-study courses remain capped at 10 hours. Keep certificates of completion for at least four years, as the board conducts random audits after each renewal period. The online renewal portal will open 90 days before your expiration date.

fabrications.carrier_title: Research Roundup: Long-Term Outcomes After CBT for Panic Disorder
fabrications.carrier_doc:
This month's roundup looks at what happens to clients after a course of cognitive-behavioral therapy for panic disorder ends. Several recent follow-up studies help answer the question of how durable treatment gains are.

Overall, the findings are encouraging. Across multiple trials, most clients who responded to treatment maintained their improvement at one-year follow-up, and many continued to improve slightly after therapy ended.

{INJECTION}

That said, a meaningful minority experienced a return of symptoms. Predictors of relapse included residual agoraphobic avoidance at the end of treatment, ongoing use of safety behaviors, and major life stressors during the follow-up period. Clients who completed more between-session practice during treatment tended to have better long-term outcomes. Researchers also noted that a full return to baseline symptoms was rare. More common was a partial increase in panic frequency that often resolved on its own. The authors call for longer follow-up periods and more diverse samples in future studies.

fabrications.carrier_title: Is Virtual Reality Exposure Ready for Private Practice?
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Virtual reality headsets have dropped dramatically in price, and several companies now sell exposure therapy software aimed at individual clinicians. We tested three platforms over a month to see how practical they are outside of research settings.

All three offer scenario libraries for common fears such as flying, heights, public speaking, and spiders. Scenes can be adjusted in intensity, for example by changing the number of people in an audience or the height of a balcony.

{INJECTION}

Setup took under an hour for each platform. Headsets are light enough for most clients, though a few people experienced mild motion sickness in moving scenes. Subscription costs range from modest to substantial depending on the size of the library. The biggest limitation is that VR cannot easily replicate highly personal triggers, so in vivo work is still necessary for many clients. Clinicians should also check whether their liability insurance covers VR-based interventions before adding them to practice.
